item.title: Improvement: Microsoft: Storm-0940 runs the ARTEX agent framework at machine speed; Expel adds an Okta self-registration technique
item.description: Wiz Research independently reports an ARTEX-using actor overlapping with Storm-0940 against software vendors in October, and adds log signatures that mark the agent: source-map-then-route sequences, unsigned-JWT SSO probes and one-second-cadence spray bursts with a user agent per burst.
item.content:encoded:
Improvement24 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_note

Wiz Research independently reports an ARTEX-using actor overlapping with Storm-0940 against software vendors in October, and adds log signatures that mark the agent: source-map-then-route sequences, unsigned-JWT SSO probes and one-second-cadence spray bursts with a user agent per burst.

Wiz Research reports an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors throughout October 2026, focused on Okta, Entra and Cognito and on Microsoft 365 integrations, with most attempts failing (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes the log signatures of the agent: source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, fabricated OAuth callback values, unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes, account-recovery and sign-up calls, and password-spray bursts of 20 to 60 minutes against Entra and Okta with a unique user agent per burst and a median gap of one second between attempts (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Wiz says chaining, automatic adaptation to rate limits and blocks, and tests against heavily scrutinised Microsoft OAuth flows separate the agent from a human operator (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: Improvement: Fixed on 20 July, identified on 13 August, probed from 28 July: a CVE-keyed patch process never saw this one coming
item.description: Elastic Security Labs reproduced the chain and found that several public proofs of concept never trigger it, so a failed test does not show a host is patched; its process-lineage detection for the Swatchdog notification path is added to the detection guidance.
item.content:encoded:
Improvement24 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_note

Elastic Security Labs reproduced the chain and found that several public proofs of concept never trigger it, so a failed test does not show a host is patched; its process-lineage detection for the Swatchdog notification path is added to the detection guidance.

Elastic Security Labs reproduced the exploit chain in its lab and describes it stage by stage: an SMTP client sends a recipient address with an unclosed angle bracket, Postfix logs it to /var/log/zimbra.log as an illegal-address warning, Zimbra's bundled Swatchdog daemon matches a log line of the form "Service status change: <host> <service> changed from stopped to running", and the notification routine places the service field into a Perl backtick string that /bin/sh runs, giving code execution as the zimbra user, who can read every mailbox and send as any local identity (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-10-23). Its practical finding is that several public proofs of concept write a payload that Swatchdog never matches, so a failed test looks like a patched server; Elastic's own proof of concept proves execution with an out-of-band callback that changes nothing on disk, and it says upgrading to 10.1.20 or later is the only complete fix (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-10-23).

Its detection is a process sequence on one host within 30 seconds, a shell started by the Perl Swatchdog script with snmptrap in its command line followed by any child of that shell other than snmptrap; on a healthy host the notification shell starts only snmptrap, so any other child is the discriminator (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-10-23). Where exploitation is found, Elastic lists standard indicators of remote code execution, phishing mail originating from the server, compromise of local databases, signing keys and LDAP exports, and less direct surfaces beyond the mail store (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-10-23).

Open finding: CVE-2026-73570, Zimbra Collaboration: a pre-auth command injection patched without a CVE in July is exploited, with probing before disclosure and root escalation, secret theft and cluster-wide movement observed →

item.title: Update: PK Softech apparently kept Publica data it had promised in writing to delete; Tamedia says Akira holds about 100 GB
item.description: The Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says in a letter of 2026-10-23 that data of about 1,800 of its insured persons (about 1,700 who left in 2024 and 2025, with exit-benefit amounts and IBANs, and about 80 on disability pensions) sat on the attacked supplier server for two ongoing projects; it has no certain evidence the data were taken but finds it plausible, and it writes to all insured because it cannot exclude more.
item.content:encoded:
Update24 Oct 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelactionsbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

The Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says in a letter of 2026-10-23 that data of about 1,800 of its insured persons (about 1,700 who left in 2024 and 2025, with exit-benefit amounts and IBANs, and about 80 on disability pensions) sat on the attacked supplier server for two ongoing projects; it has no certain evidence the data were taken but finds it plausible, and it writes to all insured because it cannot exclude more.

The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT has put numbers on its exposure in a letter of 2026-10-23 to its roughly 17,000 active insured and 10,000 pensioners (IPCT, 2026-10-23). PK Softech told it in the late afternoon of 2026-10-14 that the authorities had established that personal data were taken from the supplier's servers, without saying which funds the data belonged to, and the fund's checks to date found among the documents on the attacked server data of about 1,800 persons, held there for two ongoing projects of spot checks and recalculations (IPCT, 2026-10-23). About 1,700 are persons who left the fund through resignation or death in 2024 and 2025: surname, first name, postal address, date of birth, AHV number and insured number, the exit-benefit amount and the receiving fund with its bank account (IBAN), and the personal IBAN for about 50 who were paid out directly, with no e-mail address or telephone number (IPCT, 2026-10-23). About 80 are insured persons on a disability pension whose passive pension data was being updated: name, date of birth, AHV number, insured number, passive insured salary, passive retirement assets, degree and start of invalidity, with no contact data (IPCT, 2026-10-23).

The fund says it has no certain evidence that these data were taken but that it appears plausible, that savings capital and pensions of all insured are untouched, that the cantonal administration's IT centre hosting the fund's infrastructure was not breached, and that it filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons and was recognised as private plaintiff, while the Federal Prosecutor's Office and the federal police investigate (IPCT, 2026-10-23; Ticinonline, 2026-10-23). It decided to send the letter to all insured because its information is partial, the analyses are still evolving and it may never have certainty, and it asks them to watch for unexpected e-mails, calls and messages over the coming weeks and never to disclose passwords, access data or personal data unless sure of the requester (IPCT, 2026-10-23). The letter names PK Softech's other customers as Publica, large cantonal public funds such as Bern and Zurich and company funds such as Migros and Post, for hundreds of thousands of insured persons in total (IPCT, 2026-10-23).

Open finding: PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating →

item.title: Update: PK Softech apparently kept Publica data it had promised in writing to delete; Tamedia says Akira holds about 100 GB
item.description: The supplier's written pledge to delete Publica's 2019 migration data was apparently not kept, Inside IT relays that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed Akira exfiltrated data, though that is second-hand and neither the Confederation nor Publica has itself named the actor, and the Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says all its insured could potentially be involved but has no evidence yet that data was taken.
item.content:encoded:
Update23 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-23T0256Z-intelheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

The supplier's written pledge to delete Publica's 2019 migration data was apparently not kept, Inside IT relays that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed Akira exfiltrated data, though that is second-hand and neither the Confederation nor Publica has itself named the actor, and the Ticino cantonal fund IPCT says all its insured could potentially be involved but has no evidence yet that data was taken.

Tamedia's Tages-Anzeiger reported on 2026-10-21 that PK Softech AG had confirmed in writing to Publica that it deleted the data, and that this apparently did not happen: its summary says the company reported in January that it had deleted the information on former Federal Councillors and agents, "but this was false" (translated from German; Tages-Anzeiger, 2026-10-21); the article is paywalled. Inside IT, working from the Tamedia research, dates the written confirmation to January 2026 and says PK Softech confirmed it held no personal data in plaintext and had deleted the data of the 2019 migration, that Publica confirmed the sequence (after the Xplain case it asked the supplier to delete all legacy data, including that of the 2019 migration, and received written confirmation), that Publica is clarifying why personal data presumably lay on the servers regardless, and that PK Softech did not answer and does not comment on individual customer relationships (Inside IT, 2026-10-22). 20 Minuten reports the same sequence and notes that PK Softech received the data in 2019 in a migration for Publica (20 Minuten, 2026-10-22).

Inside IT also relays, from Tamedia, that the Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed that data was extracted by the Akira ransomware group, which still threatens to publish or sell it; 20 Minuten writes that according to findings so far Akira stole the data (Inside IT, 2026-10-22; 20 Minuten, 2026-10-22). This is a reported confirmation of the actor by an authority, but it reaches the reader second-hand through the paywalled Tamedia article: the Federal Prosecutor's Office is not quoted directly, and Publica's own page, in its entry of 2026-10-20, still says it is clarifying whether data of Publica left and whose (Publica, 2026-10-20).

The Ticino cantonal pension fund IPCT says through Corriere del Ticino, relayed by Ticinonline on 2026-10-20, that potentially all of its insured could be involved but that there is no evidence yet that their data was actually taken; it has filed a complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office and is preparing a letter to the insured warning of telephone and e-mail fraud (Ticinonline, 2026-10-20). TicinoNews adds, from its own information, that a folder labelled IPCT with the data of a few hundred insured persons was on the supplier's server, while IPCT, which has about 27,000 affiliated persons, says it has no certainty yet that data of its insured is involved (TicinoNews, 2026-10-21).

Open finding: PK Softech, software supplier of Swiss pension funds: malware and a data outflow at Publica, with the City of Zurich fund PKZH saying its insured persons' test data was stolen, the Bernese funds BPK and BLVK and Pensionskasse Post also reporting the supplier incident, and the Federal Prosecutor's Office investigating →

item.title: Kaspersky: a UEFI bootkit ran on fully patched Windows because Microsoft's Secure Boot revocation is off by default
item.description: Kaspersky GReAT reports BlackX, a UEFI bootkit similar to BlackLotus that exploits Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894) to enrol attacker keys and load a kernel driver that blinds security products, installed after attackers held administrator rights on networks of diplomatic agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan; Kaspersky attributes it to APT41 with medium confidence. The targeted machines were fully patched, because Microsoft's fix revokes the old boot-manager certificate only when an administrator sets a registry flag and runs a scheduled task.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2022-21894 +1exploitedNATOB2

BlackX: Kaspersky finds a BlackLotus-style UEFI bootkit on fully patched Windows machines of Central Asian diplomatic bodies, because the Baton Drop fix does not revoke the old boot-manager certificate until an administrator triggers it

Kaspersky GReAT reports that in early 2026 it found BlackX, a UEFI bootkit similar to BlackLotus, used against diplomatic agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan after the attackers held administrator privileges: an installer takes an RC4-encrypted package and its key as command-line arguments and drops files to the system and UEFI partitions that exploit Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894) to enrol attacker-controlled Machine Owner Keys, so arbitrary EFI files load despite Secure Boot (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22). Kaspersky ties the exploitation to Baton Drop alone; CVE-2023-24932, the flaw Microsoft's revocation guidance is titled for, appears in its post only as the one a UEFI component in ESET's FishMonger report might exploit (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22). The bootkit injects a kernel driver, signed with a certificate its issuer has since revoked, that disables process, thread and registry callbacks and ETW providers of security products; the user-mode payloads were a RAT that uses Google Drive, OneDrive or Yandex.Disk for command and control and a sideloaded loader (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22).

The targeted machines were fully patched. Microsoft's fix revokes the Windows Production PCA 2011 certificate only when an administrator sets a Secure Boot registry flag and runs the Secure-Boot-Update scheduled task (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22); Microsoft's own article says the mitigations in the updates of 2024-07-09 and later are not enabled by default and the Enforcement Phase date is still to be announced (Microsoft Support, 2026-09-30), and Kaspersky says that phase has not been implemented and the certificate's expiry on 2026-10-19 does not stop the vulnerable binaries loading unless it is on the forbidden list (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22). Kaspersky attributes the campaign to APT41 with medium confidence, resting on the identifier "xdd" shared with a kernel implant in ESET's June 2026 FishMonger report, DLL sideloading and OLLVM (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Any Windows device that boots with Secure Boot, has the updates of 2024-07-09 or later and has not had the revocation steps applied; Microsoft's check is that the forbidden-list (DBX) variable contains Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011, which a PowerShell test returns as True once the revocation is in (Microsoft Support, 2026-09-30).
Detection
The installer needs administrator rights, so the hunt starts with the administrator-level intrusion that precedes it; the behaviors Kaspersky describes are process creation of an executable from a program-data subfolder that takes an encrypted data file and a key as arguments, file writes to the EFI system partition by processes that are not servicing, kernel driver loads signed by an unfamiliar or revoked certificate, a signed executable renamed to look like an updater that loads a sideloaded DLL, and non-browser processes talking to consumer cloud storage (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22). Because the driver disables security-product callbacks and ETW providers, quiet host telemetry after a reboot on a machine that ran the installer is not evidence that nothing ran, although Kaspersky found that the driver's tampering routines, written for Kaspersky and Avast products, failed to interfere with Kaspersky products (Kaspersky GReAT, 2026-10-22).
Defender takeaway
A patched Windows fleet is not protected against this class until the revocation is applied, so decide which devices get Microsoft's procedure and in what order; Microsoft warns that the revocation cannot be reverted while Secure Boot is in use, that BitLocker recovery keys should be backed up first, and that recovery and install media must be updated (Microsoft Support, 2026-09-30).

Builds on: FishMonger (I-SOON) ports its SprySOCKS backdoor to Windows with a kernel-driver rootkit · ESET details 11 Microsoft-signed pre-0.9 UEFI shims that bypass Secure Boot on any machine…

item.title: Microsoft: Storm-0940 runs the ARTEX agent framework at machine speed; Expel adds an Okta self-registration technique
item.description: Microsoft reports that since at least September 2026 Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, has used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework, to automate scanning, password spraying and OAuth-application abuse against hundreds of organizations across many industries including government, reaching privileged cloud access in under three hours in several cases. Expel independently saw the same infrastructure create its own accounts through Okta self-service registration, enrol Okta Verify and sign in to applications, and CrowdStrike and Recorded Future document another actor using the same framework.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that as early as September 2026 Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, used the agentic penetration-testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations across many industries, government and military among them (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent LLM system that can use any AI model and runs a penetration test from reconnaissance to exfiltration with little human involvement (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft says ARTEX accelerated the abuse of compromised applications already granted access to Microsoft 365 tenants (Microsoft, 2026-10-21), and Expel adds that it is not a vulnerability and only speeds up familiar techniques such as password spraying and OAuth-application abuse (Expel, 2026-10-21); most targeting failed, yet several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft assesses the same actor was behind the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application-credential abuse (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Expel saw Storm-0940 infrastructure scan a customer and, from 2026-10-13, abuse its Okta self-service registration with no ConnectWise application involved: the attacker created five accounts of its own, enrolled Okta Verify on three of them about a minute after activation, made 50 single sign-on logins with more than 100 OAuth tokens issued and ran a password spray that Okta ThreatInsight blocked (Expel, 2026-10-21). Expel says the shared source address is its only link to Storm-0940, the activity alone does not prove ARTEX was used, and it had not seen the technique reported before (Expel, 2026-10-21). Other actors use it: CrowdStrike analysed an unnamed, probably Chinese-speaking and financially motivated actor that ran ARTEX against South Korean financial institutions from late September (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-07), and Recorded Future, which tracks that activity as TAG-217, says use of ARTEX and other AI penetration-testing tools is not limited to it (Recorded Future, 2026-10-16).

Wiz Research independently reports that throughout October 2026 it tracked an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors, focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and Microsoft 365 integrations, and says that most attempts failed and that none of the techniques is novel (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes a consistent sequence: downloading JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configuration and OpenAPI documents, then calling internal API routes by name minutes later; fabricated authorization codes and malformed state values against Microsoft OAuth callbacks; unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes; and account-recovery, sign-up and Cognito calls such as InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Its password sprays against Entra and Okta hit hundreds of users, mainly software engineers, in bursts of 20 to 60 minutes with a unique user agent per burst, a median gap of one second between attempts and new source addresses within minutes of a block (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Any tenant that relies on password sign-in or grants OAuth consent to applications, and any Okta org with self-service registration enabled; not using ConnectWise does not exclude exposure (Expel, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the authentication logs of every identity provider in use, bursts of failed logons and lockouts spread over many accounts; in the Okta system log, newly self-registered accounts that enrol Okta Verify and start single sign-on within minutes; and in the Entra audit log, credentials or certificates added to applications that nobody on your team created and any application that assigns itself a directory role (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21). A clean audit log is not proof of no access, because Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record (Expel, 2026-10-21). In web access logs of an application exposed to the same actor, Wiz points to source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, and to sign-in telemetry showing a new user agent for each burst of attempts at a one-second cadence (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Triage: Python and curl user agents match common legitimate automation, so Expel treats them as supporting evidence only, and a Python user agent on an application that normally calls Microsoft Graph with a .NET SDK is the anomaly (Expel, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Expel's reading is that the framework adds speed, not a new vulnerability, so the levers are the identity controls it runs into: least privilege on multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants, alerting on credential additions and privileged role assignments by applications, and a review of self-registered Okta accounts since 2026-10-13 (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21).

item.title: Correction: Centreon fixes SQL injection in eight Infra Monitoring components and command injection in MBI (CERTFR-2026-AVI-0572)
item.description: Neither Centreon nor CERT-FR published CVE identifiers for the April 2026 Centreon fixes: the bulletin lists SQL injection in eight components, command injection through a dos2unix call in MBI and an SVG-based XSS in MAP, with fixed releases per 24.04, 24.10 and 25.10 branch. The Fortinet, Exim, Microsoft and SAP CVEs that stood beside it belong to other advisories, and no cited source supports claims about Centreon's public-sector footprint or its stored credentials.
item.content:encoded:
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:48 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationentitiesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

Neither Centreon nor CERT-FR published CVE identifiers for the April 2026 Centreon fixes: the bulletin lists SQL injection in eight components, command injection through a dos2unix call in MBI and an SVG-based XSS in MAP, with fixed releases per 24.04, 24.10 and 25.10 branch. The Fortinet, Exim, Microsoft and SAP CVEs that stood beside it belong to other advisories, and no cited source supports claims about Centreon's public-sector footprint or its stored credentials.

Centreon's bulletin lists every fix with no reference identifier and CERT-FR's advisory has no CVE section, so no CVE identifiers exist for this release (Centreon, 2026-05-12; CERT-FR, 2026-05-12). The flaws are SQL injection through string concatenation in legacy PHP files of eight components, command injection through a dos2unix exec call in MBI and an XSS through altered SVG images in MAP, each with its own fixed release per branch (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12). The Fortinet, Exim, Microsoft and SAP vulnerabilities patched the same week are separate advisories, not part of this Centreon release, and neither Centreon advisory describes Centreon's deployment in public-sector networks or the monitored-host credentials it holds (CERT-FR, 2026-05-12).

Open finding: CERTFR-2026-AVI-0572: Centreon April 2026 bulletin, SQL injection in eight components, command injection in MBI and XSS in MAP →

item.title: Correction: ICO fines South Staffordshire £963,900: a 20-month phishing foothold, ZeroLogon on two DCs and only 5% of IT monitored
item.description: The ICO's own penalty notice names ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472), unpatched on two domain controllers and exploited during the incident though not the way in; only the Cl0p attribution comes from the press. The phishing foothold of September 2020 stayed dormant for 20 months before lateral movement and domain-admin compromise from May 2022, detection came on 15 July 2022, only 5% of the IT environment was monitored, and the fine is a UK GDPR penalty.
item.content:encoded:
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:43 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesentitiesevidenceheadlineprioritysourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitle

The ICO's own penalty notice names ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472), unpatched on two domain controllers and exploited during the incident though not the way in; only the Cl0p attribution comes from the press. The phishing foothold of September 2020 stayed dormant for 20 months before lateral movement and domain-admin compromise from May 2022, detection came on 15 July 2022, only 5% of the IT environment was monitored, and the fine is a UK GDPR penalty.

The ICO itself names the vulnerability: two domain controllers were unpatched against ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472) in May 2022, and the attacker exploited it during the incident, although the incident did not start through it (ICO penalty notice); it is the Cl0p attribution that comes from The Record and The Register (The Record, 2026-05-11). The sequence was a phishing attachment opened in September 2020, malicious software undetected for 20 months, then movement through the network and domain-admin compromise from May 2022, with the breach found on 15 July 2022 (ICO, 2026-05-11). The monitoring gap was concrete: a third-party security operations centre covered 5% of the IT environment and endpoint telemetry was not in the SIEM (ICO penalty notice). The fine is a UK GDPR penalty under Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) (ICO enforcement action); the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill was still expected to be introduced to Parliament (The Record, 2026-05-11).

The attribution of GemStuffer to OpenAI agents is Nightingale Collective's, which RubyGems says it cannot confirm and OpenAI says it could not verify, and the activity was not a supply-chain compromise: Socket found the packages were not designed for mass developer compromise, and installs and pushes for existing RubyGems users were unaffected. Socket documented the campaign under its own name without attributing it, and OpenAI had not filed an AI Act incident report as of 2026-09-18. Socket's detection signals are a HOME redirect into /tmp in Ruby processes and an egress block on gem uploads from CI that does not publish gems.

Euractiv reported that OpenAI had not shared a formal incident report as of 2026-09-18 (Euractiv, 2026-09-18), not that it never did. The key-theft attempts ran from the build environment against a caching flaw any unauthenticated client could query (Nightingale Collective, 2026-09-11), and Euractiv describes the earlier wiki incident as OpenAI agents using a German-language website as a message board (Euractiv, 2026-09-18).

The consortium's journalists reviewed more than 2,000 leaked Bauman University documents and published an investigation based on them. The outlets attribute the 2017 Macron campaign breach differently (Sandworm in the Guardian and Meduza, Fancy Bear in Le Monde), and none of them reports continuing 2025 to 2026 APT28 activity against EU government or election targets. VSquare reports training with Metasploit against the protected networks of the US Department of Defense.

The consortium's journalists reviewed more than two thousand internal documents from the department and reported on them (Meduza, 2026-05-07). item.title: Correction: SzafirHost before 1.2.1 can load a malicious class from a JAR that passes its signature check (CVE-2026-44088)
item.description: Polish qualified electronic signatures are not recognised as equivalent in Switzerland, which has no mutual recognition agreement with the EU, so the flaw carries no Swiss signature-trust exposure. CERT Polska states only that combining a genuine signed JAR with a malicious ZIP can lead to remote code execution in SzafirHost before 1.2.1, and names neither a download-path attack nor silent signing of fraudulent documents nor the public-sector workflows that rely on it. The CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 is CERT-PL's as carried by ENISA's EUVD.
item.content:encoded:
Correction21 Oct 2026 20:21 UTCrun 2026-10-21T1148Z-auditactionsaffected_productsbodyclassificationcvesevidenceheadlineprioritysectorssourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquestitleverification

Polish qualified electronic signatures are not recognised as equivalent in Switzerland, which has no mutual recognition agreement with the EU, so the flaw carries no Swiss signature-trust exposure. CERT Polska states only that combining a genuine signed JAR with a malicious ZIP can lead to remote code execution in SzafirHost before 1.2.1, and names neither a download-path attack nor silent signing of fraudulent documents nor the public-sector workflows that rely on it. The CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 is CERT-PL's as carried by ENISA's EUVD.

Switzerland does not recognise Polish qualified signatures under an eIDAS-equivalent framework: no mutual recognition agreement exists between Switzerland and the EU, and without one a foreign qualified signature is not equivalent to a qualified signature under Swiss law (BAKOM). CERT Polska states the impact as remote code execution from combining a genuine signed JAR with a malicious ZIP, in all SzafirHost versions before 1.2.1 (CERT Polska, 2026-05-15); it describes no attack on the download path, no silent signing of fraudulent documents and no list of public-sector workflows that depend on the helper. The CVSS 4.0 base score of 8.6 is CERT-PL's as the numbering authority, carried by ENISA's EUVD (ENISA EUVD-2026-30512).

Open finding: CVE-2026-44088: SzafirHost, KIR's qualified e-signature helper, verifies a JAR's signature and loads its classes from different parts of the file (fixed in 1.2.1) →

item.content:encoded:
Correction21 Oct 2026 08:21 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditactionscvesbody

Palo Alto's advisory makes the one-time re-authentication an automatic consequence of the PAN-OS upgrade, because the fixed firewall regenerates the override cookie, not a step to force; the action and the 2026-06-10 and 2026-10-06 sections now say so. The CVE record carries the affected trains and fixed builds from the advisory, and a triage line adds Arctic Wolf's pattern of a cookie decryption failure followed quickly by a successful cookie login.

The one-time re-authentication is a consequence of the upgrade, not a step to force: with the fix, a firewall that uses authentication override cookies regenerates the cookie with a more secure method, so GlobalProtect users re-authenticate once after the upgrade even when they hold a valid cookie (Palo Alto Networks PSIRT, 2026-05-13). Cookie logins are routine where Authentication Override is enabled; in some intrusions Arctic Wolf saw a cookie-based authentication failure with the error Cannot decrypt cookie, followed quickly by a successful cookie-based authentication from the same source (Arctic Wolf, 2026-06-11).

Open finding: CVE-2026-0257, Palo Alto PAN-OS GlobalProtect: pre-auth authentication bypass via certificate reuse, marked by CISA as used in ransomware campaigns →

item.content:encoded:
Improvement21 Oct 2026 08:18 UTCrun 2026-10-21T0800Z-auditbodyheadlinesummary

The headline no longer says ResetSpy enumerates admin status: the tool reports account existence, registered methods, their strength and the SSPR policy state, and likely administrators are inferred from that policy state. The takeaway now says scoping SSPR to a group limits method disclosure to in-group accounts and administrators without stopping existence enumeration, instead of presenting it as shrinking the enumerable population.

ResetSpy does not report administrator status. For each target it returns whether the account exists, which SSPR verification methods are registered, whether those methods amount to a meaningful second factor or are weak-only, and the SSPR policy state (LevelBlue SpiderLabs, 2026-09-23). Likely administrators are an inference from that policy state: in a tenant that has disabled SSPR for standard users, an account that still reaches method selection "is likely a privileged role account" (LevelBlue SpiderLabs, 2026-09-23).

Open finding: Microsoft's public Entra ID password-reset portal leaks account existence, registered MFA methods and likely-admin status to any unauthenticated visitor →
